cast

KAST · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To cast is to project or direct something outward, such as a shadow, a glance, or doubt.

The new evidence cast doubt on the timeline the detectives had built.

Example

The oak tree cast a long shadow across the lawn just before sunset.

The tree projected its shadow outward onto the lawn. Casting is sending something out from a source -- here a shadow, but it works the same way for light, glances, blame, and doubt.

How Strong Is It?

aim → cast → hurl

aim vs. cast

aim vs. cast: To aim only points something in a direction -- to cast actually sends it out: light, glances, doubt.

hurl vs. cast

hurl vs. cast: To hurl is pure force -- a violent throw. Cast can mean throw too, but usually with control or purpose, like casting a fishing line.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cast: to throw (kasta) (Old Norse)

Put it together: Cast came whole from Old Norse kasta, 'to throw' -- there are no Latin or Greek pieces to take apart. English kept the throwing image and stretched it: you can cast a net, but also cast a shadow, a glance, or doubt -- throwing something outward from yourself.

Use the root in a new word: broadcast: Early radio pioneers chose the farming word broadcast -- 'to scatter seed widely' -- for sending a signal out in all directions.

Strength Check

Word Choice

The ISEE loves the extended sense: cast doubt, cast blame, cast a shadow -- projecting something outward. Cast can also simply mean to throw with force ('he cast the net into the sea'); both are correct. The theater sense (casting actors) and the mold sense are different uses -- set them aside for now.
